preamble: In Latin, Proto-Indo-European *dʰ developed into /b/ word-internally when adjacent to *r, before *l, or after *u. The path ran through a Proto-Italic voiceless fricative *θ (voiced medially to *ð), which became labial *f/*β and finally the stop b. Word-initially *dʰ gave Latin f (fūmus 'smoke'), and elsewhere medially d (medius 'middle'). The shift is effectively confined to Latin: the Sabellic languages have f in the same words (Umbrian uerfale beside Latin verbum).

examples.note: After r. Cognate with English word and Umbrian uerfale (with f).
Before r. Cognate with Ancient Greek ἐρυθρός and Sanskrit rudhirá.
After u and before r. Cognate with English udder.

sources: Sihler, A. L. (1995). New Comparative Grammar of Greek and Latin. Oxford University Press. ISBN 0-19-508345-8
